newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia opens 16 new blocks to foreign mining.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia opens 16 new blocks to foreign mining.

text.p: Mongolia will open 16 new blocks of land to foreign investors for mineral development and exploration under new favourable conditions, senior government officials said.
"Formulation of a unified national mineral policy is in full swing," said L. Nyamsambuu, minister of Agriculture and Industry.

"We intend to expand the exploration area from the currently granted 12.7 percent, up to 40 percent of the total territory (of Mongolia) in the near future," he told business officials, mostly from the mining and energy sectors, at a conference.

Currently more than 50 companies with foreign investment operate in Mongolia's mining sector, and a total area of 136,000 square km (52,496 square miles) -- or 8.7 percent of Mongolia's land area -- has been granted for exploration by foreign companies, he said.

Among the investors are Britain's Rio Tinto Plc, KOJEMA of France, Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co and Zarubejtsvetmet of Russia, he said at the conference late last week. He gave no details of the size of their investment.

Ulan Bator will open 16 new blocks to foreign investors, including seven believed to hold gold deposits and one with potential for copper and gold, while the others could yield zinc, uranium or silver.
Mongolia has rich gold, copper, zinc, uranium and silver deposits, much of it yet to be exploited, as well as good prospects for oil, officials have said.

Mongolia would invite foreign investment in several fields, such as developing deposits already found, exploring in areas of high potential, investing in local companies and buying assets and shares soon to be available through privatisation of state-owned firms, Nyamsambuu said.
"More importance has been attached to creating a favourable and attractive environment for investment and providing legally guaranteed long term stable conditions," he said.
Foreign investment was welcome in mining infrastructure, leasing and management of equipment, the insurance and banking sectors and information services, he said.
Investors would from now on have access to all mineral and geological information, he said. Previously, Mongolia released only a limited amount of data.
Mongolia would soon set up a Mineral Authority under the Ministry of Agriculture and Industry to grant exploration and mining licences, he said.

Initial exploration licences would be granted for up to three years, with the right to renew twice for periods of two years. The licence would allow all types of exploration survey in a block and give the priority right to development, he said.

Mining licences would be issued for a 60-year period, which could be extended for 40 years. A single licence would cover an area of 4,000 square km (1,544 square miles) and there would be no restrictions on the number of licences granted to a single company.
A new mineral law, to be approved soon by parliament, would reduce the royalty rate to 2.5 percent of revenue, down from 12.5 percent, for all minerals, the minister said.

Investors who invested more than $2.0 million over a five-year period would be entitled to establish a special Stability Agreement with the Ministry of Finance, he said, but gave no details of what the agreement entailed.
Investors would also enjoy tax breaks, such as exemption of infrastructure development costs from tax and an accelerated depreciation of fixed assets.
Mongolia plans to reduce the business income tax to a maximum 30 percent from next year. Some businesses now pay 40 percent.
Investors would be able to import all machinery, equipment, materials and services duty free, he said.
